intro: In Ogi Park, in Saga Prefecture, a Buddhist pine has been clipped into a cube for generations. It is called the kaku-maki, the squared maki, and local tradition puts it at about 350 years old, a figure no survey has checked. It holds no natural monument status, yet visitor information for the park still names it among the things to see. The park is public, open all year, and free as far as any source mentions.
meta_description: The kaku-maki of Ogi Park, Saga: a Buddhist pine clipped into a cube for generations, about 350 years old by local tradition.
question_meta: Ogi Park's kaku-maki is a Buddhist pine clipped into a cube, about 300 to 350 years old by local tradition, in Saga Prefecture.
question_answer: The kaku-maki in Ogi Park, Saga Prefecture, is a Buddhist pine (inumaki) pruned by generations of gardeners into the shape of a cube; kaku-maki means squared maki. Local tradition gives its age as about 350 years, with published figures between 300 and 350. It is not a designated natural monument, but current visitor information for the park still names it among the things to see.
question_context: Ogi Park is in the town of Ogi, in Saga Prefecture on the island of Kyushu, and it counts among Japan's 100 notable historic parks. The kaku-maki grows inside the park. Its fame is not size but discipline: a crown that has been cut square by one gardener after another, for generations. The age of about 350 years is tradition rather than measurement, and we have found no survey behind it, so treat it as the park's story about itself. A photograph from December 2017 shows the tree in place, and visitor information gathered up to January 2026 still lists the 350-year-old kakumaki as a feature. The park is open all year and no source mentions a ticket. Being an evergreen, the tree looks much the same in every season, so there is no best month for it, only the park's own seasons around it. Our pin comes from where a photographer stood, so it is close rather than exact; once inside the park, the square crown is easy to pick out. No train or bus time from Saga has been checked.

trees.story:
This tree has been clipped into a box. Its name says so: kaku-maki means squared maki, and the maki in question is an inumaki, a Buddhist pine, pruned by generation after generation of gardeners until the crown became a cube.

Local tradition puts it at about 350 years old, and the published range runs from 300 to 350. That figure is tradition, not a measurement, and we have found no survey behind it. What is certain is the work: a shape like this does not happen once, it lasts only as long as somebody keeps cutting it, and here somebody has, for generations.

It grows in Ogi Park in Saga Prefecture, one of Japan's 100 notable historic parks. The tree itself carries no natural monument designation. Current visitor information for the park, gathered up to January 2026, still names the 350-year-old kakumaki among the things to see, and a photograph from December 2017 shows it in place.

The park is public, open all year, and no source mentions a ticket. Our pin comes from where a photographer stood, so it is close rather than exact; inside the park, the square crown is the giveaway.

Nobody has published a recent girth or height. If you measure it, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, clipped into a square block, which is what kaku-maki means. It stands inside Ogi Park; the pin is close rather than exact, so look for the cube.
